title: Purity, Concentration and Chromatography
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Chemistry
summary: What purity means and how to calculate it, how concentration depends on the number of solute particles in a volume, and how to carry out and read paper chromatography.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Know that purity describes how much of one particular chemical is in a sample. (8Cm.04)
Understand that the concentration of a solution depends on how many solute particles are in a volume of the solvent. (8Cp.01)
Describe how paper chromatography separates the substances in a sample and helps identify them. (8Cp.02)

blocks.text: 2. What does "pure" mean in science?

In everyday language "pure" often means "natural" or "with nothing added" — a carton may say "100% pure orange juice". In science, a **pure substance contains only one chemical**. Orange juice contains water, sugars, acids and vitamins, so a scientist calls it a **mixture**.

Most real samples are not perfectly pure. They contain small amounts of other substances called **impurities**. **Purity** describes **how much of the specific chemical you want is in the sample**. A sample that is 99% pure is almost all the wanted chemical; one that is 60% pure contains a lot of other substances.

rows: Impurities could be harmful, so medicines must be extremely pure and are tested carefully.
Tap water is not pure (it has dissolved minerals) but it must be free from harmful impurities such as microorganisms and toxic metals.
24 carat gold is pure gold. 18 carat gold is 18/24 = 75% gold; other metals are added to make it harder.
Salt from the sea is purified to remove sand and other salts.

blocks.text: 3. Calculating percentage purity
When you know the mass of the wanted chemical in a sample, you can work out its purity as a percentage:

blocks.title: Formula
blocks.text: **percentage purity = (mass of the wanted chemical ÷ total mass of the sample) × 100**

items: Find the mass of the wanted chemical (sometimes you must subtract the mass of the impurities first).
Divide by the total mass of the sample.
Multiply by 100 and write the % sign.

blocks.text: You can also use particles: if 16 out of 20 particles are the wanted substance, purity = 16 ÷ 20 × 100 = 80%.

blocks.title: How do scientists check purity?
blocks.text: A pure substance melts and boils at **fixed** temperatures. For example, pure water boils at 100 °C (at normal air pressure) — salty water boils at a higher temperature. So if a sample melts or boils at a different temperature, or over a range of temperatures, it is probably impure. Chromatography (section 6) is another check: a pure substance gives only **one** spot.
4. Concentration of a solution

When a **solute** (such as sugar) dissolves in a **solvent** (such as water) it makes a **solution**. The solute particles spread out between the solvent particles. The **concentration** tells you **how many solute particles there are in a certain volume of solvent**.

items: **More** solute particles in the **same volume** → **more concentrated**.
The **same** number of solute particles in a **bigger volume** → **more dilute** (less concentrated).
To **dilute** a solution, add more solvent. The number of solute particles stays the same, but they are spread through more liquid.
To make a solution **more concentrated**, dissolve more solute in it, or evaporate some of the solvent.
For a coloured solution, a more concentrated solution usually looks **darker** (more coloured particles in each cm³).

blocks.text: **Comparing concentrations with numbers.** Always compare the mass of solute in the **same volume**. For example, 10 g of sugar in 50 cm³ of solution is the same concentration as 20 g in 100 cm³ (double both). 15 g in 100 cm³ is less concentrated than that.

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية
blocks.text: النقاء (purity) = قد إيه من المادة اللي إحنا عايزينها موجود في العينة. المادة النقية فيها نوع واحد بس من الجسيمات. التركيز (concentration) = عدد جسيمات المذاب في حجم معين من المذيب: جسيمات أكتر في نفس الحجم = محلول مركز أكتر. لو زودت ماء، عدد جسيمات المذاب مش بيتغير، لكن بتتوزع في حجم أكبر فيبقى المحلول مخفف أكتر.
5. How paper chromatography works

Many coloured substances — inks, food colourings, plant dyes — are really **mixtures** of several dyes. **Paper chromatography** separates them so you can see how many substances are present and identify them.

blocks.alt: Paper chromatography of black ink showing red and green bands
blocks.caption: Black ink after paper chromatography: the solvent has carried its dyes up the paper and separated them into red, green and dark bands, so the ink is a mixture.
blocks.credit: Photo: Oscar / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 540 315" width="540" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13"><rect x="140" y="58" width="200" height="10" fill="#e3f4e5" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M150 70 L150 300 L330 300 L330 70" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="151" y="262" width="178" height="37" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="0"/><line x1="150" y1="262" x2="330" y2="262" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.2"/><rect x="152" y="76" width="176" height="6" fill="#d9d9d9" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="215" y="82" width="50" height="206" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.3"/><line x1="218" y1="245" x2="262" y2="245" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.3"/><ellipse cx="230" cy="245" rx="5" ry="4" fill="#0f1b33"/><ellipse cx="250" cy="245" rx="5" ry="4" fill="#0f1b33"/><line x1="340" y1="63" x2="365" y2="63" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1"/><text x="370" y="67">lid</text><line x1="265" y1="150" x2="365" y2="150" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1"/><text x="370" y="154">chromatography paper</text><line x1="328" y1="79" x2="365" y2="79" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1"/><text x="370" y="83">glass rod</text><line x1="255" y1="245" x2="365" y2="245" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1"/><text x="370" y="249">spots of the samples</text><line x1="330" y1="282" x2="365" y2="280" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1"/><text x="370" y="284">solvent (below the line)</text><line x1="120" y1="245" x2="217" y2="245" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1"/><text x="10" y="241">pencil start</text><text x="10" y="257">line</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Paper chromatography apparatus.

items: Draw a **start line** in **pencil** about 2 cm from the bottom of the chromatography paper. (Pencil does not dissolve, so it will not move or add spots.)
Put a **small, concentrated spot** of each sample on the line, spaced apart. Label each one in pencil under the line.
Pour a little **solvent** (often water or ethanol) into a beaker. Hang the paper so the bottom dips into the solvent but the **solvent level is below the start line**.
Cover the beaker with a **lid** so the solvent does not evaporate.

The solvent soaks up the paper. As it passes the spots, it **dissolves** the substances and carries them upwards. Substances that are **more soluble** in the solvent travel **further**; less soluble ones travel a shorter distance.

Take the paper out **before the solvent reaches the top**. Mark how far the solvent got (the **solvent front**) in pencil, then let the paper dry. The dried paper with its spots is the **chromatogram**.

blocks.alt: Four felt-tip ink samples separating on paper hanging in a beaker of water
blocks.caption: Paper chromatography of four inks. The pencil start line is above the water, and each ink separates into different coloured dyes as the water soaks up the paper.
blocks.credit: Photo: Pbak4622 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0

blocks.title: Safety
blocks.text: Ethanol is flammable — keep it away from flames. Wear eye protection, and do not touch the spots or eat the food colourings used.
6. Reading a chromatogram

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 480 310" width="480" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13"><rect x="30" y="30" width="360" height="270" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="30" y1="250" x2="390" y2="250" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.3"/><line x1="30" y1="60" x2="390" y2="60" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text x="396" y="64">solvent</text><text x="396" y="80">front</text><text x="396" y="254">start</text><text x="396" y="270">line</text><ellipse cx="66" cy="117" rx="9" ry="7" fill="#0f1b33"/><text x="66" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">A</text><ellipse cx="138" cy="202.5" rx="9" ry="7" fill="#0f1b33"/><text x="138" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">B</text><ellipse cx="210" cy="155" rx="9" ry="7" fill="#0f1b33"/><text x="210" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">C</text><ellipse cx="282" cy="202.5" rx="9" ry="7" fill="#0f1b33"/><ellipse cx="282" cy="117" rx="9" ry="7" fill="#0f1b33"/><text x="282" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">X</text><ellipse cx="354" cy="250" rx="9" ry="7" fill="#0f1b33"/><ellipse cx="354" cy="155" rx="9" ry="7" fill="#0f1b33"/><text x="354" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">Y</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Chromatogram of three known dyes A, B and C, and two unknown samples X and Y (same paper, same solvent).

items: **Each spot is one substance.** The number of spots tells you the (minimum) number of substances in a sample. X has 2 spots, so it contains at least 2 substances.
**A pure substance gives one spot.** A, B and C each give one spot, so each could be a single substance.
**Same height = same substance** (on the same paper with the same solvent). X has spots level with A and B, so X contains **A and B**. Y has a spot level with C, so Y contains **C**.
**A spot left on the start line** is a substance that is **insoluble** in this solvent — it did not move. Y contains an insoluble substance as well as C.
If a spot in the unknown matches **none** of the known samples, the unknown contains a substance that was not tested.

blocks.text: Chromatography is used to identify food colourings, to check if a medicine is pure, to test athletes for banned substances, and by forensic scientists to match the ink on a document to a particular pen.
7. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — A 40 g sample of rock salt contains 2 g of sand. The rest is salt. Calculate the percentage purity of the salt. [2]

items: Mass of salt = 40 − 2 = 38 g.
Purity = (38 ÷ 40) × 100 = **95%** (1 mark working, 1 mark answer).
**Common mistake:** using the 2 g of sand: (2 ÷ 40) × 100 = 5% is the percentage of **impurity**, not the purity.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — A particle diagram of a gas sample shows 25 particles: 20 are oxygen and 5 are nitrogen. (a) Is the oxygen pure? [1] (b) Calculate the percentage purity of the oxygen. [1]

items: (a) **No** — it contains nitrogen particles (an impurity) as well as oxygen.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — Solution A has 10 g of salt in 50 cm³. Solution B has 15 g of salt in 100 cm³. Which is more concentrated? Show how you decide. [2]

items: Make the volumes the same: A = 10 g in 50 cm³ = **20 g in 100 cm³**. B = **15 g in 100 cm³** (1).
20 g > 15 g in the same volume, so **A is more concentrated** (1).
**Common mistake:** choosing B because 15 g is more than 10 g, without looking at the volume.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — Explain, using particles, what happens to the concentration of a squash drink when you add more water. [2]

items: The number of solute (squash) particles stays the **same** (1).
They are spread through a **larger volume** of water, so there are fewer solute particles in each cm³ — the drink becomes **more dilute** (less concentrated) (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Use the chromatogram in section 6. (a) How many substances are in X? [1] (b) Which known dyes are in X? [1] (c) What does the spot on the start line for Y show? [1]

items: (a) **2** (two spots).
(b) **A and B** — X's spots are at the same heights as A's and B's spots.
(c) Y contains a substance that is **insoluble** in the solvent, so it did not move.
**Exam tip:** say "at the same **height**" or "travelled the same **distance**" — not just "the same".

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Omar sets up chromatography. He draws the start line in felt-tip pen and pours the solvent in until it is 1 cm **above** the line. Describe **two** mistakes and explain why each is a problem. [4]

items: Mistake 1: the line is in **ink** (1). The ink would dissolve and separate into its own spots, mixing with the results (1).
Mistake 2: the solvent is **above** the start line (1). The samples would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker instead of moving up the paper (1).
**Exam tip:** a "describe and explain" question needs **what** is wrong **and why** — 2 marks each.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Calling a natural product like "pure honey" or "pure juice" a pure substance — in science these are mixtures.
Working out the percentage of **impurity** when the question asks for the **purity**.
Comparing concentrations without making the volumes the same.
Thinking that adding water removes solute particles — the number of solute particles stays the same.
Confusing **dilute** with **dissolve**. Dissolve = the solute mixes into the solvent; dilute = add more solvent.
Saying a spot on the start line "was not tested" — it means the substance is **insoluble** in that solvent.
Drawing the start line in ink, or letting the solvent cover the spots.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Draw particle diagrams** of a pure substance and an impure sample (use different shapes or shading and a key).
**Calculate** a percentage purity — show the division and the × 100.
**Circle** the most concentrated / most dilute solution from particle diagrams or from masses and volumes.
**Explain** dilution using the words particles, same number, larger volume.
**Label** the chromatography apparatus and **explain** why the line is in pencil and the solvent is below it.
**Read a chromatogram**: how many substances, which known dyes match, which sample is pure, which contains an insoluble substance.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Purity, concentration and chromatography — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: Which of these is a **pure substance** in the scientific meaning of the word?
questions.e: Distilled water contains only water particles — one substance — so it is pure. Sea water (water + salts), orange juice (water, sugars, acids…) and air (nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide…) are all mixtures. A juice can be called "100% pure" on a label, but in science it is still a mixture.

questions.q: A 25 g sample of impure copper sulfate contains 24 g of copper sulfate. Calculate the percentage purity of the sample.
questions.e: percentage purity = (mass of copper sulfate ÷ total mass of sample) × 100 = (24 ÷ 25) × 100 = **96%**. 1 mark for the correct division, 1 mark for the answer.

questions.q: Pure gold is called 24 carat. A ring made of 18 carat gold contains 18 parts gold out of every 24 parts. What percentage of the ring is gold?
questions.e: 18 ÷ 24 = 0.75; 0.75 × 100 = **75%**. The other 25% is other metals (such as copper or silver), which are the 'impurities' here — they make the ring harder.

questions.e: All four have the same volume, so the most concentrated is the one with the **most solute particles**: B has 9 (A has 3, C has 6, D has 4).

questions.q: Ali has 100 cm³ of sugar solution. He adds 100 cm³ of water. Which statement is correct?
c: The number of sugar particles stays the same, so the solution becomes less concentrated.
The number of sugar particles goes down, so the solution becomes less concentrated.
The number of sugar particles stays the same, so the concentration stays the same.
The solution becomes more concentrated because there is more liquid.
questions.e: Adding water (solvent) does not remove any sugar particles. The **same number** of solute particles is now spread through a **bigger volume** (200 cm³), so there are fewer particles in each cm³ — the solution is **more dilute** (less concentrated).

questions.p:
Question 6
Solution P: 12 g of salt dissolved to make 50 cm³ of solution.
Solution Q: 20 g of salt dissolved to make 100 cm³ of solution.
questions.q: Which solution is more concentrated? Write P or Q.
questions.e: Compare the same volume. P: 12 g in 50 cm³ = 24 g in 100 cm³. Q: 20 g in 100 cm³. 24 g > 20 g, so **P** is more concentrated. Common mistake: choosing Q because 20 g is more than 12 g — but Q also has twice the volume.

questions.q: Why is the start line on chromatography paper drawn in **pencil**, not in ink?
c: Pencil (graphite) does not dissolve in the solvent, so it does not move up the paper.
Ink would stop the solvent moving up the paper.
questions.e: Graphite is insoluble in the solvent, so the pencil line stays where it is. Ink is a mixture of dyes that would dissolve and separate, adding extra spots that would spoil the results.

questions.q: (a) How many different substances are there in ink X?
questions.e: X makes **3** separate spots, so it contains at least 3 different substances (each spot is one substance).

questions.q: (b) Which **two** inks were mixed to make ink X? Write two letters.
questions.e: X has spots at the same heights as P's spot and **both** of Q's spots, so X contains **P and Q**. It cannot contain S: S leaves a spot on the start line, and X has no spot there. R's spot is at a height where X has no spot.

questions.q: (c) Which ink contains a substance that is **insoluble** in this solvent? Write one letter.
questions.e: An insoluble substance does not dissolve, so the solvent cannot carry it up the paper — it stays **on the start line**. Only **S** has a spot on the start line.

questions.q: (d) Which **two** inks could each be a single, pure substance? Write two letters.
questions.e: A pure substance gives **one** spot. P and R each give only one spot. Q and X give more than one spot, and S has two (one on the start line), so they are mixtures.

questions.q: Explain why the level of the solvent must be **below** the start line at the beginning of a chromatography experiment. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: otherwise the spots/samples would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker (wash off the paper). 1 mark: so they would not move up the paper / would not separate / the results would be lost. Do not accept 'so the paper does not get wet'.
questions.e: If the solvent were above the start line, the samples would **dissolve straight into the solvent in the beaker** instead of being carried up the paper, so they would **not separate** and there would be no chromatogram to read.

questions.q: Draw two particle diagrams, each in a box with 10 particles: (a) a pure substance; (b) a sample that is 80% pure. Use a key. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: (a) all 10 particles drawn the same. 1 mark: (b) 8 particles of one type and 2 particles of a different type (8 out of 10 = 80%), with a key showing the two types. Accept particles touching or not touching (solid, liquid or gas arrangement is not marked).
questions.e: (a) Ten identical circles — one substance only. (b) 80% of 10 = 8, so draw **8** particles of the wanted substance and **2** of a different-looking particle (the impurity). Add a key, e.g. ○ = substance, ● = impurity.

questions.q: Mona has two copper sulfate solutions. Solution 1 is pale blue and solution 2 is dark blue. Both have the same volume. Use ideas about particles to explain the difference. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: solution 2 is more concentrated. 1 mark: it has more (copper sulfate) solute particles in the same volume (of water/solvent). Accept reverse argument for solution 1 (fewer particles in the same volume, more dilute).
questions.e: Solution 2 is **more concentrated**: it has **more copper sulfate particles in the same volume** of solvent. More coloured particles in each cm³ make the colour darker.

blocks.title: Remember
items: A pure substance contains only one chemical. Purity = how much of the wanted chemical is in a sample.
Percentage purity = mass of wanted chemical ÷ total mass × 100.
Concentration = how many solute particles are in a volume of solvent. Adding solvent dilutes; the number of solute particles stays the same.
Chromatography: pencil start line, small spots, solvent below the line, lid on. More soluble substances travel further.
One spot = one substance; same height = same substance; a spot on the start line = insoluble in that solvent.
